explanations.explanation: Ahijah it is, and Jeroboam names him himself in verse 2. Back in 1 Kings 11:29-31, Ahijah the Shilonite met Jeroboam on the road and tore a new cloak into twelve pieces. Now Jeroboam is sending his wife to that same prophet.
Nathan is a real prophet, but his name goes with David's days. The LORD sent him to David in 2 Samuel 12:1. In this passage the prophet in Shiloh is Ahijah, and he's the one Jeroboam names.

Shemaiah is a real prophet, called the man of God in 1 Kings 12:22, but that word came to Rehoboam's day. Here Jeroboam points to the prophet in Shiloh, and the text names him as Ahijah. Lots of prophet names in this part of the Bible, friend, and I mix them up too.

The boy, friend. Jeroboam says it plainly in verse 3: "He will tell you what will become of the boy." His son Abijah is sick, and that's the whole reason for the trip. I think that tells you where Jeroboam's heart is right now.

Kingdom is a fair guess, since kingdoms are all over the chapters around this one. But verse 3 says the prophet will tell her what will become of the boy. The sick son is the reason for the trip (1 Kings 14:1), and the kingdom isn't what Jeroboam is asking about.
No army in this scene, friend. Verse 3 says the prophet will tell her what will become of the boy. Abijah is sick, and that's why she's heading to Shiloh. The soldiers can wait for another story.

The LORD told him. Verse 5 says He let Ahijah know that Jeroboam's wife was coming about her sick son, and that she would be disguised. Ahijah can't see a thing, but he got the full report from the One who can. So that disguise was walking into a plan it never knew about.

Not the king. Jeroboam is the one who sent her in disguise, so he's the last person tipping off Ahijah. Verse 5 says it was the LORD who spoke to Ahijah ahead of time. The news was already waiting before she reached the door.

Servant is close to something true, since verse 18 calls Ahijah "His servant." But verse 5 doesn't mention anybody running ahead with a message. It says the LORD said it to Ahijah. The word came straight from God.
That's not what verse 5 says. The LORD tells Ahijah, "You are to say such and such to her…" So she isn't getting a closed door. She's getting a message, even if it's a hard one.

False, and you caught it. In verse 5 the LORD tells Ahijah, "You are to say such and such to her…" so he has a message ready. She won't leave without an answer. I think it's an answer she won't want, though.

True, and he doesn't waste a second. He hears her at the door and says, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam! Why are you disguised?" (1 Kings 14:6). Somebody at the costume shop is getting a strongly worded review.
He does greet her that way. Verse 6 has Ahijah say, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam! Why are you disguised?" He knew who she was as soon as he heard her. I'd ask for a refund on that costume.

Ahijah says it in his own words: "…I have been sent to you with bad news." (1 Kings 14:6). She came for an answer about her son, and he doesn't dress it up. I think that's a heavy thing to hear at a door.
No peace news here, friend. In verse 6 Ahijah says, "…I have been sent to you with bad news." The rest of the passage shows how heavy it is. It's a hard word to bring about her son.

Victory would be a nice thing to hear at a door, but that's not what he brings. In verse 6 Ahijah says he has been sent with "bad news." Nothing in this scene is a victory lap. It's a heavy part of the story, friend.

explanations.answer: Followed God with all his heart
explanations.explanation: In verse 8 God speaks through Ahijah, and He says David "…kept My commandments and followed Me with all his heart, doing only what was right in My eyes." That's the measure God holds up. It's about David's heart following Him. Heart first, friend, always.

explanations.answer: Built God a temple in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Building the temple was Solomon's job. 1 Kings 6:1 says he began building the house of the LORD in the fourth year of his reign. In verse 8, God is talking about David keeping His commandments and following Him with all his heart. A building isn't what He points to there.

explanations.answer: Brought the ark home to Shiloh
explanations.explanation: David did bring up the ark of God to the City of David (2 Samuel 6:12), but that's not Shiloh, and it isn't what God names here. Verse 8 points to David keeping God's commandments and following Him with all his heart. Shiloh is where Ahijah is in this story, but the ark isn't part of God's message.

True, and God doesn't soften it: "You have done more evil than all who came before you." (1 Kings 14:9). That's a heavy sentence, friend. It comes right after God reminds Jeroboam in verses 7 and 8 of what he was given.

It's actually true. In verse 9 God says to Jeroboam through Ahijah, "You have done more evil than all who came before you." That's a heavy line, friend. The verse goes right on to name other gods and molten images.

In verse 9 God speaks to Jeroboam through Ahijah: "You have proceeded to make for yourself other gods and molten images to provoke Me…" Molten images are idols cast from metal. So "other gods and metal idols" is exactly what God names. Jeroboam made them, and God says they were to provoke Him.

Ships sound like something a big kingdom would build, but this passage never mentions them. In verse 9 God says Jeroboam made "…other gods and molten images…" Those are the things He names in His message. Trading ships don't show up anywhere in it.

A cedar palace sounds like something a king would build, but verse 9 says no such thing. God says Jeroboam made "…other gods and molten images…" Those are the things He names. A palace isn't in His message at all.

explanations.answer: Cut off every male in it
explanations.explanation: God says to Jeroboam through Ahijah, "I will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both slave and free, in Israel…" (1 Kings 14:10). That's a heavy line, friend. I think this one hurts.
Verse 10 doesn't say anything about Egypt. God says He will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both slave and free. It's a cutting off, not a move. That's a heavy line, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: Make it serve the house of David
explanations.explanation: Verse 8 does mention the house of David, as the one the kingdom was torn from. But in verse 10 God says He will cut off every male belonging to Jeroboam. Nothing there is about serving anybody. I think it's a hard sentence.

explanations.answer: When her feet enter the city
explanations.explanation: Ahijah says it in verse 12: "When your feet enter the city, the child will die." I think this is the hardest line in the whole passage. She hears it in Shiloh, and then she has to go home. Verse 17 says it happened as she stepped over the threshold of the house.

That's not what Ahijah says. In verse 12 he first tells her to get up and go home. Then he says the child will die when her feet enter the city. So it comes after she leaves Shiloh, not before. I think that's a hard thing to be told.

No number of days is given. Ahijah ties it to her feet entering the city in verse 12: "When your feet enter the city, the child will die." Verse 17 shows it happening as she steps over the threshold of the house. I think that's a heavy thing to hear.

Ahijah says the opposite. In verse 13 he says, "All Israel will mourn for him and bury him." It's not just the family. Verse 18 says it happened, and all Israel mourned. That's a lot of people grieving for one boy.

False, and good catch. Ahijah says, "All Israel will mourn for him and bury him." (1 Kings 14:13). Verse 18 says they buried him and all Israel mourned. That's a whole nation grieving, and it's a heavy moment.

explanations.answer: The LORD found some good in him
explanations.explanation: Ahijah tells her in verse 13 that this boy is the only one belonging to Jeroboam who will receive a proper burial, "…because only in him has the LORD, the God of Israel, found any good in the house of Jeroboam." Out of a whole house, one boy is singled out. I think that's a quiet kindness tucked inside a hard message.

The text never says Abijah was the firstborn, so that isn't the reason it gives. In verse 13 Ahijah says it's "…because only in him has the LORD, the God of Israel, found any good in the house of Jeroboam." The reason is what the LORD found in him. Nothing is said about where he stood in the family.

explanations.answer: He asked for the prophet's help
explanations.explanation: His mother is the one who makes the trip, and nothing in the text says Abijah asked anyone for anything. In verse 13 Ahijah gives the reason: "…because only in him has the LORD, the God of Israel, found any good in the house of Jeroboam." The reason is what the LORD found in him. It isn't something the boy asked for.

True. In verse 14 Ahijah says the LORD "…will raise up for Himself a king over Israel who will cut off the house of Jeroboam." The king is raised up for the LORD Himself. That matches verse 10, where the house of Jeroboam was already named in the disaster.

Ahijah says it will. In verse 14 he says the LORD "…will raise up for Himself a king over Israel who will cut off the house of Jeroboam." The king is raised up for the LORD Himself. Verse 10 had already named the house of Jeroboam in the disaster.

explanations.answer: A reed shaken in the water
explanations.explanation: Ahijah says the LORD will strike Israel "…as a reed is shaken in the water." (1 Kings 14:15). I think the picture is of something that can't hold steady when the water moves it. That's a shaky place to stand.

explanations.answer: A lamp snuffed out at night
explanations.explanation: There's no lamp in this message, friend. In verse 15 Ahijah says the LORD will strike Israel "…as a reed is shaken in the water." The picture is a reed and water. Nothing about a lamp or the night.

explanations.answer: A jar smashed on the ground
explanations.explanation: No broken jar in this message. In verse 15 Ahijah says the LORD will strike Israel "…as a reed is shaken in the water." It's a reed in water, not a jar on the ground. Nothing gets smashed in that picture.

In verse 15 Ahijah says the LORD will uproot Israel "…from this good land that He gave their fathers…" The land was a gift to those who came before them. To be uprooted from a gift is a heavy thing, I think.

Prophets get lots of lines in this chapter, since one is doing the talking. But in verse 15 Ahijah says the land is the one "…that He gave their fathers…" The word there is fathers, not prophets. The land came to them first, and the message is about Israel being uprooted from it.
No priests in this message. In verse 15 Ahijah says the land is the one "…that He gave their fathers…" The land was given to the fathers. The message is about Israel being uprooted from it.

Ahijah says in verse 16 that God will give Israel over "…on account of the sins Jeroboam has committed and has caused Israel to commit." That's two things: what Jeroboam did and what he led Israel into. Verse 15 names the Asherah poles Israel made, provoking the LORD to anger.
Rehoboam is Solomon's son, who became king after him (1 Kings 11:43). He's in the story, but verse 16 doesn't name him. It names the sins "…Jeroboam has committed and has caused Israel to commit."

Solomon is a name from earlier in the story, and he's gone by now. 1 Kings 11:43 says he rested with his fathers and Rehoboam reigned in his place. Ahijah's words in verse 16 are about "…the sins Jeroboam has committed and has caused Israel to commit."

True. Verse 17 says, "…as soon as she stepped over the threshold of the house, the boy died." Ahijah had told her the child would die when her feet entered the city (1 Kings 14:12). It's a heavy moment, friend.

It does happen at that moment. Verse 17 says, "…as soon as she stepped over the threshold of the house, the boy died." Ahijah had told her the child would die when her feet entered the city (1 Kings 14:12). It's a heavy line, and I won't pretend otherwise.
Verse 20 says, "…his son Nadab reigned in his place." Jeroboam's reign lasted twenty-two years, and then he rested with his fathers. After that the throne goes to Nadab.
Omri isn't in this passage. Verse 20 says Jeroboam's son Nadab reigned in his place. Keep an eye out for who's named, friend.
Rehoboam is a king, but he's Solomon's son (1 Kings 11:43), not Jeroboam's. Verse 20 names Nadab as the son who reigned in Jeroboam's place. Two kings, two sons, and it's easy to mix them up.
